items.title: Origin of the Kushanas — the Yue-Chi
items.body:
## A Central Asian Tribe

- The Kushanas were a **Central Asian tribe** originating from the **Yue-Chi (Yuezhi) Confederation**.
- They gradually established dominance over **Gandhara, the Kabul Valley, and the Indus Basin**, expanding their empire into **India and Central Asia**.
- Their reign marked significant **cultural, religious, economic, and artistic transformations**, shaping ancient Indian history profoundly.
- **Kujula Kadphises (I)** united the Yue-Chi tribes and founded the Kushana empire.
keyPoints: Kushanas = a Central Asian tribe from the Yue-Chi (Yuezhi) Confederation.
Established dominance over Gandhara, the Kabul Valley and the Indus Basin.
Expanded the empire into both India and Central Asia.
Kujula Kadphises (I) united the Yue-Chi tribes and founded the empire.
Their rule brought major cultural, religious, economic and artistic change.
items.mnemonic: Roots — 'Kushanas came from the Yue-Chi', Central Asia to the Indus.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (overview; Key Rulers)

items.title: The Kadphises Kings — Foundation & Gold Coins
items.body:
## Kujula & Vima Kadphises

- **Kujula Kadphises I (15 CE – 64 CE)** united the Yue-Chi tribes, **established the Kushana empire**, and issued **Roman-inspired gold coins**.
- **Vima Kadphises II (64 CE – 78 CE)**:
  - **Expanded the empire to Mathura and the Indus basin**.
  - **Issued large quantities of gold coins**.
  - Was a **devotee of Shiva** (Shaivite leanings on his coinage).
- The Kadphises rulers laid the political and economic base that **Kanishka I** would later expand.
keyPoints: Kujula Kadphises I (15–64 CE): founded the empire; issued Roman-inspired gold coins.
Vima Kadphises II (64–78 CE): expanded to Mathura and the Indus basin.
Vima Kadphises II issued large quantities of gold coins.
Vima Kadphises II was a devotee of Shiva.
The Kadphises kings set the base for Kanishka I's expansion.
items.mnemonic: Two Kadphises — 'Kujula founds, Vima expands (to Mathura) & mints gold'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Key Rulers of the Kushana Empire)

items.title: Kanishka I — The Greatest Kushana
items.body:
## Kanishka I (78 CE – 105 CE)

- Kanishka I began his reign in **78 CE**, the year traditionally taken as the start of the **Saka era** (with which he is credited as founder).
- **Empire's extent:** spanned from **Central Asia to the Ganges valley** and from **Khorasan to Varanasi**.
- **Twin capitals:** ruled from **Purushapura (Peshawar)** and **Mathura**.
- **Religious patronage:** **Mahayana Buddhism became prominent**; he built **Buddhist stupas and monasteries** across the empire.
- Adopted the divine title **"Devputra" (Son of God)**, highlighting the divine nature of kingship.

figure.alt: Map of the Kushan Empire showing Purushapura (Peshawar), Gandhara, Mathura and trade routes to the Ganges valley
figure.caption: The Kushan Empire under Kanishka I — stretching from Central Asia to the Ganges valley, with capitals at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, straddling the Silk Route.

keyPoints: Kanishka I reigned 78–105 CE; 78 CE marks the start of the Saka era (credited as founder).
Empire ran from Central Asia to the Ganges valley, Khorasan to Varanasi.
Ruled from twin capitals: Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura.
Made Mahayana Buddhism prominent; built stupas and monasteries.
Adopted the divine title 'Devputra' (Son of God).
items.mnemonic: Kanishka '78' — Saka era begins; capitals 'Purushapura + Mathura'; title 'Devputra'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Kanishka I: Key Contributions)

items.title: Fourth Buddhist Council & the Rise of Mahayana
items.body:
## The Council in Kashmir

- Kanishka I **organised the Fourth Buddhist Council** in **Srinagar, Kashmir**.
- It was **presided over by Vasumitra** (with **Ashvaghosha** traditionally associated as a leading scholar).
- The council **marked the division between Mahayana and Hinayana Buddhism**.
- Under Kanishka's patronage **Mahayana Buddhism flourished** and spread to **China and Central Asia**.

figure.alt: Gandhara-school seated Buddha carved in grey stone with Hellenistic drapery
figure.caption: Mahayana Buddhism gained ground under Kanishka; the era's Gandhara art gave the Buddha a Graeco-Roman form.

keyPoints: Kanishka convened the Fourth Buddhist Council at Srinagar, Kashmir.
Presided over by Vasumitra; Ashvaghosha associated as a leading scholar.
Marked the split between Mahayana and Hinayana Buddhism.
Mahayana Buddhism flourished and spread to China and Central Asia.
items.mnemonic: 4th Council = 'Kashmir + Kanishka + Vasumitra' → Mahayana vs Hinayana split.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Kanishka I: Fourth Buddhist Council; Religion and Society)

items.title: Schools of Art — Gandhara, Mathura & Amravati
items.body:
## Three Schools of Art

Kanishka and the Kushanas promoted the **Gandhara** and **Mathura** schools of art; the contemporary **Amravati** school flourished in the south under the Satavahanas/Ikshvakus.

| Feature | Gandhara | Mathura | Amravati |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Theme** | Predominantly Buddhist | Hindu, Buddhist & Jain deities | Jataka tales & Buddha's life |
| **Style** | Realistic, Hellenistic influence | Indigenous, bold, muscular | Narrative art, intricate reliefs |
| **Material** | Blue-grey stone | Red sandstone | White marble-like stone |
| **Patrons** | Kushanas | Kushanas | Satavahanas, Ikshvakus |
| **Locations** | Gandhara, Bamyan | Mathura, Kankalitila | Amravati, Nagarjunakonda |

- **Gandhara:** Buddha depicted with **Greek drapery and wavy hair**.
- **Mathura:** **robust figures with Indian motifs** in red sandstone.

figure.alt: Mathura-school seated Buddha carved in red sandstone with robust Indian features
figure.caption: Mathura School: robust, indigenous figures in red sandstone — contrasting with the Hellenistic grey-stone Gandhara Buddha.

keyPoints: Kushanas patronised the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
Gandhara: blue-grey stone, Hellenistic Buddha with Greek drapery and wavy hair.
Mathura: red sandstone, indigenous robust figures with Indian motifs.
Amravati (Satavahana/Ikshvaku patrons): white marble-like stone, narrative Jataka reliefs.
Locations — Gandhara/Bamyan, Mathura/Kankalitila, Amravati/Nagarjunakonda.
items.mnemonic: Art schools — 'Gandhara = Grey & Greek, Mathura = Maroon (red) & Muscular, Amravati = white Marble & narrative'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Three Schools of Art)

items.title: Court Scholars & Literary–Scientific Contributions
items.body:
## The Learned Court of Kanishka

- **Ashvaghosha:** composed **Buddhacharita**, a biography of the Buddha (Sanskrit literature).
- **Charaka:** the **father of Ayurveda**, was **patronised by Kanishka** (medical advancement).
- **Vatsyayana:** composed the **Kamasutra** during this period, reflecting societal norms and values.
- **Astronomy/astrology:** Greek influences introduced terms such as **horoscope**.
- These contributions made the Kushana court a hub of Sanskrit learning, medicine and science.
keyPoints: Ashvaghosha wrote the Buddhacharita, a biography of the Buddha.
Charaka, father of Ayurveda, was patronised by Kanishka.
Vatsyayana composed the Kamasutra in this period.
Greek influence introduced astronomical/astrological terms like 'horoscope'.
The court was a centre of Sanskrit literature, medicine and science.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Scientific and Literary Contributions)

items.title: Administration — Satraps & Dual Rule
items.body:
## Governing a Vast Empire

- The empire was divided into **Satrapies (provinces)**, each governed by a **Mahakshatrapa (chief satrap)** — a military governor who was **both administrator and military commander**.
- **Districts** were run by **Dandanayaka / Mahadandanayaka** (semi-military officials).
- **Villages** were managed by **Gramika / Padrapala** (village headmen) responsible for **tax collection and law and order**.
- **Dual hereditary rule:** two rulers held power concurrently, sharing responsibilities to maintain stability over the vast empire.
- The satraps also secured **trade routes**, protecting movement along the **Silk Route**.
keyPoints: Provinces = Satrapies, each under a Mahakshatrapa (chief military governor).
Districts run by Dandanayaka / Mahadandanayaka (semi-military officials).
Villages run by Gramika / Padrapala (headmen) — tax collection and law & order.
Dual hereditary rule: two rulers shared power concurrently for stability.
Satraps defended trade routes along the Silk Route.
items.mnemonic: Ladder of rule — 'Mahakshatrapa → Dandanayaka → Gramika' (province → district → village).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Administration of the Kushana Empire)

items.title: Coinage, Economy & the Silk Route
items.body:
## Trade and Money

- Issued **gold, silver, and copper coins** in large quantities:
  - **Gold** — trade; featured **Shiva, Buddha, and Greek gods like Zeus**.
  - **Silver** — regional trade; depicted **Kushana rulers**.
  - **Copper** — daily use; images of **temples and local symbols**.
- Coins featured **Greek, Hindu and Buddhist deities**, reflecting **religious tolerance**, and adopted **Roman coin standards** to promote trade.
- **Economy:**
  - Controlled the **Silk Route**, facilitating **Indo-Roman trade** and generating **toll revenue**.
  - Promoted **agriculture** with **irrigation systems in Afghanistan and Pakistan**.
  - **Imported** silk and spices; **exported** gold, precious stones and ivory.
keyPoints: Issued gold, silver and copper coins in large quantities.
Gold coins featured Shiva, Buddha and Greek gods like Zeus; adopted Roman standards.
Controlled the Silk Route — Indo-Roman trade plus toll revenue.
Promoted agriculture with irrigation in Afghanistan and Pakistan.
Imported silk & spices; exported gold, precious stones and ivory.
items.mnemonic: Coins G-S-C — 'Gold (trade), Silver (regional), Copper (daily)'; wealth from the Silk Route.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Coinage and Economy of the Kushanas)

items.title: Religion & Society — Pluralism under the Kushanas
items.body:
## A Tolerant, Plural Society

- **Mahayana Buddhism** flourished with Kanishka's patronage, spreading Buddhism to **China and Central Asia**.
- **Hindu influence:** rulers like **Vima Kadphises** were **devotees of Shiva**; some Kushanas also supported **Vaishnavism**.
- **Religious tolerance:**
  - Coins depicted **multiple deities**, showing a **pluralistic society**.
  - **Stupas and temples for different faiths** were built across the empire.
keyPoints: Mahayana Buddhism flourished under Kanishka and spread to China & Central Asia.
Vima Kadphises and others were devotees of Shiva; some supported Vaishnavism.
Coins depicted multiple deities — evidence of a pluralistic society.
Stupas and temples for different faiths were built across the empire.
items.mnemonic: Kushana faith mix — 'Buddha + Shiva + Vishnu on the coins' = tolerance.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Religion and Society under the Kushanas)

items.title: Decline & Legacy of the Kushanas
items.body:
## The End of Kushana Power

- **Vasudeva I (early 3rd century CE)** was the **last significant Kushana ruler**; his reign witnessed the **decline of Kushana power**.
- The **Sassanians overthrew the Kushanas in Central Asia**, while Indian territories **fragmented into smaller kingdoms**.
- **Legacy:** despite the decline, the Kushanas left a lasting mark in **art, religion and governance** — the satrap system, Gandhara/Mathura art and Mahayana Buddhism — influencing subsequent Indian dynasties.
keyPoints: Vasudeva I (early 3rd century CE) was the last significant Kushana ruler.
The Sassanians overthrew the Kushanas in Central Asia.
Indian territories fragmented into smaller kingdoms.
Legacy endured in art, religion and governance (satraps, Gandhara/Mathura art, Mahayana).
Influenced subsequent Indian dynasties.
items.mnemonic: Fall — 'Vasudeva last; Sassanians take Central Asia; India fragments'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Decline of the Kushana Empire)

items.title: Precision Facts the PYQs Hinge On (Council venue, Nagarjuna, Rajatarangini)
items.body:
## High-Yield Exam Nuggets

### Fourth Buddhist Council — the exact details
- **Venue:** **Kundalavana (Kundalvana Vihara), near Srinagar in Kashmir** (some traditions place it at Jalandhar).
- **President:** **Vasumitra**; **Deputy/Vice-President:** **Ashvaghosha**.
- It compiled the great commentary **Mahavibhasha** and finalised the **Mahayana–Hinayana** division; proceedings were recorded in **Sanskrit**.

### Court scholars — don't forget Nagarjuna
| Scholar | Known for |
|---|---|
| **Ashvaghosha** | Buddhacharita, Saundarananda (Sanskrit poet) |
| **Charaka** | Charaka Samhita — 'father of Ayurveda' |
| **Nagarjuna** | Madhyamika/Sunyavada (Doctrine of the Void) — Mahayana philosopher |
| **Vatsyayana** | Kamasutra |

### Kanishka in the sources
- **Kalhana's *Rajatarangini*** (a 12th-century Kashmiri chronicle) records **Kanishka's rule/invasion in Kashmir**.
- Kanishka's **coins and inscriptions have been found at Mathura, Sravasti, Kausambi and Sarnath (Benares)** — evidence of the empire's reach into the Ganga valley.
- The **Rabatak inscription** (Afghanistan) lists the Kushana royal genealogy (Kujula→Vima Takto→Vima Kadphises→Kanishka).
keyPoints: Fourth Buddhist Council venue = Kundalavana (near Srinagar), Kashmir; President Vasumitra, Deputy Ashvaghosha; compiled the Mahavibhasha in Sanskrit.
Nagarjuna (Madhyamika/Sunyavada — Doctrine of the Void) was a leading Mahayana philosopher of the Kushana age.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini records Kanishka's rule/invasion in Kashmir.
Kanishka's coins/inscriptions found at Mathura, Sravasti, Kausambi and Sarnath (Benares).
The Rabatak inscription (Afghanistan) gives the Kushana genealogy up to Kanishka.
items.source: Kalhana's Rajatarangini; standard NCERT/ASI facts on the Fourth Buddhist Council (Kundalavana), Nagarjuna and the Rabatak inscription
